title: A Reconnection Is Not a Recovery
subtitle: Epoch-Fenced Reacquisition and Recovery Budgets for Unattended Industrial Sensors
rights: Copyright Mark Yarian. All rights reserved; public reading and citation permitted.
abstract: Unattended industrial sensors often fail in ways that invite a simple operational response: reconnect the radio, restart the worker, or power-cycle the node. Such actions can restore a data stream while leaving its epistemic state unresolved. Buffered samples may reappear out of order; a restarted process may inherit stale calibration; a peripheral may advertise while its sensing element remains stuck; and repeated resets can deplete power or conceal a persistent fault. This paper argues that autonomous sensor recovery should be specified as a bounded, evidence-producing protocol rather than a sequence of restart commands. It proposes Epoch-Fenced Reacquisition (EFR): a per-source acquisition epoch that invalidates predecessor streams, a layered recovery ladder with persistent action budgets, and a separate warmup/validation gate before observations regain model authority. The proposal is derived from failure-detector theory, Bluetooth link semantics, operating-system watchdog and restart mechanisms, OT safety guidance, and measurement-uncertainty practice. A fault-injection protocol is specified to compare EFR against naive reconnect and service-level restart baselines. No new recovery algorithm is claimed as validated, and no autonomous firmware or hardware recovery capability is asserted for SynapticSteel TelePod. The contribution is a testable integration contract for remote sensing where physical access may be expensive or impossible.
evidence_classification: Architecture and fault-injection evaluation protocol; no measured recovery or reliability benefit.
